title: Semantic Caching, Fallbacks & OpenTelemetry
summary: This intermediate module teaches learners to distinguish prefix, exact-match, and semantic caches, configure semantic caching safely, design attributable fallback routes, and identify what telemetry needs verification. After completing it, learners can design and evaluate an auditable cache-and-fallback gateway instead of treating every cache as answer-neutral.
objectives: Distinguish prefix, exact-match, and semantic caches by what they key on, and explain how exact-match and semantic response caches can return stale answers.
Configure a semantic cache's threshold, partition, and lifetime using each tool's documented threshold semantics, and exclude multi-turn and agentic traffic that it breaks.
Design a fallback chain with retries, timeouts, cooldowns, and context-window and content-policy routes, and make fallback-served responses distinguishable after the fact.
Plan gateway telemetry while separating source-supported fields from OpenTelemetry GenAI details whose support is UNKNOWN in the supplied material.

sections.title: Three caches, keyed on three different things
paragraphs: Caching names three mechanisms with different failure modes. A prefix cache inside the engine reuses attention state: vLLM hashes each full key-value block together with its parent block's hash and extras such as LoRA IDs, and its design notes describe prefix caching as almost a free lunch that does not change model outputs because it saves prefill compute. An exact-match response cache sits in front of the model: LiteLLM's exact-match caches key on a hash of the whole request, so any change to the conversation is a miss. LiteLLM also notes that an in-memory cache lives inside one worker process, so multiple workers keep separate caches.

A semantic cache is different. LiteLLM's semantic caches embed the prompt and serve the closest cached response whose cosine similarity clears a similarity_threshold. Azure API Management's llm-semantic-cache-lookup policy returns a stored response based on the vector proximity of the prompt to previous requests and a score threshold. In either case, the user can receive an answer generated for a different request. API Management warns that similarity-based responses can be incorrect, outdated, or unsafe for the current request.

A prefix cache reuses internal state without changing the model output. A semantic cache can substitute an answer generated for a different request. An exact-match response cache can also affect the answer a user receives by replaying an outdated response for an identical request instead of performing a fresh execution. Evaluate prefix caching for latency and hit rate, exact-match caching for hit rate and staleness, and semantic caching for false hits, staleness, and unsafe cross-request reuse.
sections.callout: Prefix caching changes computation without changing model output. Exact-match and semantic response caches can replay stale answers, while semantic caching adds the risk of serving an answer generated for a different request.

sections.title: Tuning a semantic cache: threshold, partition, lifetime
paragraphs: Threshold numbers do not transfer between tools because their meanings are inverted. In API Management, score-threshold ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and lower values require higher semantic similarity. The policy reference suggests starting low, such as 0.05, and warns that a threshold above 0.2 may lead to cache mismatch. In LiteLLM, similarity_threshold is the cosine similarity a cached entry must clear, and its examples use 0.8, so higher is stricter there. Record each value beside the tool's own definition, and never copy a threshold from one product's runbook into another's configuration.

Partition by trust boundary before tuning anything else. API Management's vary-by element partitions the cache, and its example uses the caller's subscription ID. The policy reference advises controlling cross-user access by varying on user or user-group identifiers. LiteLLM documents that the semantic cache key leaves the prompt out, so tenant scope such as virtual key, team, or organization keeps callers apart. End users behind one virtual key share one bucket, and a response generated for one can be served to another who sends a similar prompt. Setting semantic_cache_scope to end_user isolates buckets per authenticated end user. vLLM provides an optional cache_salt for its prefix cache to limit reuse to requests sharing the salt and reduce timing attacks that infer cached content from latency.

A semantic cache also adds a dependency to every request. LiteLLM runs the embedding call inline and caps it at 5 seconds. After that deadline, the lookup is abandoned, the response carries x-litellm-semantic-similarity: 0.0, and the request proceeds as a miss. Increasing semantic_cache_embedding_timeout increases how long requests wait when the embedding endpoint does not answer. API Management advises sizing the embeddings deployment for prompt volume, placing a rate-limit policy immediately after lookup so the backend is protected if the cache is unavailable, and setting a duration on the paired llm-semantic-cache-store policy. The tools also differ in the text they compare: API Management recommends ignore-system-messages to remove system messages before similarity is assessed, while LiteLLM embeds the messages array, including the system prompt. Verify which text the selected tool compares before trusting a similarity score.
sections.callout: API Management: lower score-threshold is stricter. LiteLLM: higher similarity_threshold is stricter. The numbers are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Why semantic caches break multi-turn and agent traffic
paragraphs: LiteLLM documents a failure mode for multi-turn and agentic workloads, including coding agents and tool-calling loops that resend the conversation. Each new turn is the previous request plus a small appended change. Consecutive turns can therefore have embeddings around 0.99 similar, causing a turn to match the previous turn's cached entry and replay a stale response. This can appear as an agent repeating the same tool call. Raising the threshold does not reliably fix the problem, and assistant tool_calls are not part of the embedded text, making consecutive agent turns harder to distinguish.

The documented remedy is scope rather than threshold tuning. Keep semantic caching for single-shot traffic and exclude agentic traffic. LiteLLM supports exclusion by setting no-cache in metadata for the virtual keys used by agents, making caching opt-in with a default-off mode, or allowing clients to opt out per request. If agentic traffic must use a response cache, an exact-match cache ensures that a changed conversation is a miss, although an identical request can still receive a stale stored response. API Management provides a related guard in max-message-count, which skips caching after a dialog exceeds a configured number of remaining messages.

Before enabling a semantic cache, classify traffic behind each route or key as single-shot, multi-turn, or agentic. Enable semantic caching only for single-shot traffic that passes an evaluation containing prompts that must not hit. A cache that is suitable for an FAQ endpoint can be dangerous for an agent loop, so semantic caching should not be treated as a gateway-wide default.

sections.title: Fallbacks: retries, cooldowns, and honest attribution
paragraphs: A fallback chain decides what answers when the primary cannot. In LiteLLM, if a call fails after num_retries, the router tries model groups in the listed fallback order. It distinguishes content_policy_fallbacks for content-policy violations, context_window_fallbacks for context-window-exceeded errors, and fallbacks for other failures such as rate limits. Context-window routing requires enable_pre_call_checks: true. Without it, requests are sent to the provider regardless of input token count. The documented example combines num_retries: 3, a request_timeout of 10 seconds, allowed_fails: 3, and a cooldown_time of 30 seconds that temporarily removes a failing deployment from rotation.

Attribution is the part gateways can miss. LiteLLM's spend logs record attempted_fallbacks, where 0 means the requested model group served the request, and original_model_group. Both are written by the proxy and overwrite client-supplied values, so directly served and fallback-served requests remain distinguishable afterward. Its documentation also says to test fallbacks by triggering a real provider error in a non-production environment. Mock-testing flags are stripped from proxy requests as of LiteLLM Proxy v1.85.0.

A fallback serves a different model, so do not assume that evaluation results for the primary apply to it. Evaluate each fallback separately. Preserve the requested model group, the model that actually answered, and the number of fallback attempts in logs or traces. The supplied LiteLLM source establishes attempted_fallbacks and original_model_group for this purpose.

sections.title: Tracing the gateway after the OpenTelemetry source move
paragraphs: Source update: the cited OpenTelemetry GenAI material moved from its earlier location to the separate semantic-conventions-genai repository. The source records in this module now point to that repository. This update does not assert detailed attribute requirements, stability labels, metric definitions, histogram buckets, content-capture rules, or the absence of a standardized semantic-cache-hit attribute because support for those details is UNKNOWN from the supplied material.

Build an auditable gateway record from facts established elsewhere in this module. For each request, record whether the semantic cache was consulted, whether it hit, which partition was used, and which threshold interpretation applied. If a fallback runs, retain LiteLLM's attempted_fallbacks and original_model_group fields. Treat prompt and response recording as a separate data-governance decision because a semantic cache stores prompts and responses and can expose one user's stored response to another user when partitioning is too broad.

Before implementing OpenTelemetry GenAI field names, required attributes, stability labels, or metrics, verify them directly against the cited repository revision. Those details are intentionally omitted here rather than presented as established facts. The practical outcome is a telemetry plan that distinguishes source-supported gateway records from convention details that still require verification.

activity.title: Design a cache-and-fallback gateway you can audit
instructions: Classify one application's traffic into single-shot, multi-turn, and agentic classes with rough shares, and decide for each class whether to use no cache, an exact-match cache, or a semantic cache.

For the semantic-cache class, choose one of the documented tools and write down whether lower or higher threshold values are stricter. Then record a starting value from its documentation, the partition key, entry lifetime, and embedding timeout.

Build an evaluation set of at least 30 prompt pairs, including pairs that should hit and pairs that must not hit because they have similar wording but different meaning or belong to different tenants. Record which pairs the cache actually served.
Define a fallback chain with retry count, timeout, cooldown, and separate context-window and content-policy routes. Name the evaluation used to approve each fallback model.

Specify the records emitted for a request that misses the cache and is answered by a fallback. Include attempted_fallbacks and original_model_group. Mark any proposed OpenTelemetry GenAI field whose detailed definition has not been verified from the cited repository as UNKNOWN and do not implement it until verified.
evidence: A traffic-class table with the caching decision and reason for each class.
The semantic-cache configuration with the threshold's documented meaning and must-not-hit results including every false hit.
A fallback-chain table and a sample record for a fallback-served request showing attempted_fallbacks and original_model_group.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which false hit in your must-not-hit set would have caused the most harm, and which control, threshold, partition, lifetime, or traffic exclusion, stopped it?

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the three cache types?
choices: Only semantic caching can affect the answer a user receives

Prefix caching reuses internal state without changing model output, exact-match caching can replay a stale answer for an identical request, and semantic caching can serve an answer generated for a different request
Prefix caching and semantic caching always return identical fresh executions
Exact-match caching serves responses for merely similar requests
questions.explanation: Prefix caching changes computation without changing model output. Exact-match caching can replay an outdated stored response for an identical request. Semantic caching can return a response generated for a different but similar request.

questions.prompt: An API Management runbook uses score-threshold 0.05, while a LiteLLM example uses similarity_threshold 0.8. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both values have the same direction and are interchangeable
In API Management lower values require higher similarity, while in LiteLLM a cached response must clear the cosine-similarity threshold, so higher values are stricter
In both tools lower values are stricter
The two values can be compared without reading their definitions
questions.explanation: The tools define their thresholds in opposite directions, so a value from one tool must not be copied into the other without translating its meaning.

questions.prompt: Why does LiteLLM recommend excluding agentic traffic from semantic caching?
choices: Agents cannot send text
Consecutive turns are nearly identical text, so a turn can match the previous cached entry and replay a stale response
Semantic caches cannot store responses containing JSON
Agent traffic never repeats context
questions.explanation: Multi-turn agent requests often resend the preceding conversation with a small addition, making consecutive embeddings highly similar and creating stale replay risks.

questions.prompt: Under LiteLLM's documented default semantic-cache scope, what keeps two end users behind the same virtual key from receiving each other's similar cached responses?
choices: Their prompts are always included in an exact cache key
Nothing; they share a bucket unless semantic_cache_scope is set to end_user
Each network connection receives a separate cache
The embedding model automatically identifies each user
questions.explanation: The module explains that end users behind one virtual key share a semantic-cache bucket unless semantic_cache_scope is set to end_user.

questions.prompt: A LiteLLM context_window_fallbacks rule never triggers, and oversized requests reach the primary model. What does the module say is required?
choices: num_retries set to 0
enable_pre_call_checks: true
A semantic cache in front of the router
A cooldown_time longer than 60 seconds
questions.explanation: The fallback section states that context-window routing requires enable_pre_call_checks: true so input size is checked before the provider call.

questions.prompt: Which two LiteLLM spend-log fields does the module identify for attributing fallback behavior?
choices: attempted_fallbacks and original_model_group
score-threshold and vary-by
cache_salt and max-message-count
similarity_threshold and ignore-system-messages
questions.explanation: LiteLLM records attempted_fallbacks and original_model_group, allowing directly served and fallback-served requests to be distinguished.

questions.prompt: What should a learner do before implementing detailed OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute requirements from this module?
choices: Assume every gen_ai field is stable
Verify the details directly against the cited semantic-conventions-genai repository revision because those details are UNKNOWN from the supplied material
Use provider-cache fields for semantic-cache hits without checking
Infer required attributes from the LiteLLM threshold documentation
questions.explanation: The telemetry section marks detailed OpenTelemetry GenAI requirements as UNKNOWN from the supplied material and directs learners to verify the cited repository before implementation.

questions.prompt: Why should prompt and response recording be treated as a separate data-governance decision?
choices: Prompts cannot be stored
A semantic cache stores prompts and responses, and broad partitioning can expose one user's stored response to another user
Fallbacks erase all request records
Prefix caches publish their contents automatically
questions.explanation: The module connects telemetry content decisions to the same access risk as semantic-cache storage: overly broad partitions can allow cross-user response reuse.
